title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
author: John D. Lee · Katrina A. See

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Automation safety: Coordination matters beyond workload reduction
st.an: The supplied excerpts are bibliography entries only. They do not reveal the source authors’ substantive position on human–machine coordination, workload reduction, decision-centered design, or the applicability of human-factors evidence to legal AI.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the need for selective, human-centred automation and materially extends the cluster by explaining how trust calibration, interface design and operator context govern appropriate reliance. Its evidence on overtrust during multitasking strengthens the cluster’s warning that nominal human oversight may fail, while its design framework provides concrete methods for aligning reliance with task-specific capability.
qs: Good calibration, high resolution, and high speciﬁcity of trust can mitigate misuse and disuse of automation, and so they can guide design, evaluation, and training to enhance humanautomation partnerships.

A situation in which an operator has highly reliable automation, combined with the responsibility for multiple tasks in addition to monitoring the automation, can lead to overtrust in automation and undermine the detection of automation failures (Parasuraman, Molloy, & Singh, 1993).

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s argument that effective human oversight cannot be inferred from human presence, trust or professional status alone. It shows that reliance on automation varies with operating context and users’ self-confidence, reinforcing the need to design oversight around actual human decision-making conditions. It does not address expertise development or the adequacy of professional rules.
qs: Understanding the role of trust in the decision to rely on automation requires a consideration of the operating context that goes beyond trust alone.
The opposite is also true: Low self-conﬁdence is related to a greater inclination to rely on the automatic  TRUST IN AUTOMATION 71  controller (Lee & Moray, 1994).

mo.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status

kp.k: Trust supports reliance when automation exceeds human understanding
kp.d: This 2004 interdisciplinary review develops a conceptual framework for human reliance on imperfect automation, drawing on laboratory, simulator and field research in aviation, navigation, manufacturing, process control and computing. It does not discuss legal services directly. The authors argue that trust becomes particularly important when complexity, uncertainty and unanticipated circumstances make exhaustive understanding or procedural guidance impractical.
qs: Trust in automation guides reliance when the complexity of the automation makes a complete understanding impractical and when the situation demands adaptive behavior that procedures cannot guide.
The range of investigative approaches demonstrates that trust is not an artifact of controlled laboratory studies and shows that it plays an important role in actual work environments.

kp.k: Trust is an attitude, not reliance itself
kp.d: The authors distinguish beliefs, trust, intentions and observable behavior. Trust is an attitude concerning an agent's contribution to a person's goals under uncertainty and vulnerability; reliance is behavior. Workload, self-confidence, effort, time constraints and configuration problems can intervene, so observing reliance does not isolate the effect of trust.
qs: Trust can be deﬁned as the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual’s goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability.
In the context of trust and reliance, trust is an attitude and reliance is a behavior.
Trust stands between beliefs about the characteristics of the automation and the intention to rely on the automation.

kp.k: Both misuse and disuse undermine automation's benefits
kp.d: The review describes inappropriate reliance in two directions: relying on automation while violating its critical assumptions, and rejecting useful capabilities. Illustrations include failure to intervene in aircraft and ship navigation and operators rejecting paper-mill controllers. Although the framework often simplifies reliance to engagement or disengagement, the authors explicitly recognize graded reliance across multiple modes.
qs: Misuse refers to the failures that occur when people inadvertently violate critical assumptions and rely on automation inappropriately, whereas disuse signifies failures that occur when people reject the capabilities of automation.
Misuse and disuse are two examples of inappropriate reliance on automation that can compromise safety and profitability.
Automation reliance is not a simple binary process, but the simpliﬁcation makes the discussion of misuse and disuse more tractable.

kp.k: Appropriate trust requires calibration, resolution and specificity
kp.d: Calibration is correspondence between trust and capability; resolution is sensitivity to differences in capability; specificity concerns particular functions and changes over time or context. Overtrust and distrust are opposite calibration failures. The authors recommend these distinct dimensions for design, training and evaluation rather than treating higher overall trust as the objective.
qs: Calibration refers to the correspondence between a person’s trust in the automation and the automation’s capabilities (Lee & Moray, 1994; Muir, 1987).
Overtrust is poor calibration in which trust exceeds system capabilities; with distrust, trust falls short of the automation’s capabilities.
Temporal specificity reflects the sensitivity of trust to changes in context that affect automation capability.
Design for appropriate trust, not greater trust.

kp.k: Performance, process and purpose provide distinct trust foundations
kp.d: The framework distinguishes what automation does, how it operates and why it was developed. Performance includes reliability and demonstrated competence; process concerns the suitability and comprehensibility of algorithms; purpose concerns intended use and the designer's intentions. Trust also depends on consistency between observations and inferences across these dimensions. Providing information alone is insufficient unless users can assimilate it.
qs: Performance information describes what the automation does.
Process information describes how the automation operates.
Purpose describes why the automation was developed.
Trust depends not only on the observations associated with these three dimensions but also on the inferences drawn among them.
However, the mere availability of information will not ensure appropriate trust.

kp.k: Trust develops through analytic, analogical and affective processes
kp.d: The authors integrate deliberate reasoning, category-based judgments and emotional responses. They argue that rational-choice accounts can overstate cognitive capacity and understate affect. Neurological studies of decision making and cooperation provide a possible explanation for affect's role, rather than direct proof of a specific mechanism governing automation trust. Category judgments, etiquette and reputations can guide expectations but also produce inappropriate trust.
qs: Ultimately trust is an affective response, but it is also influenced by analytic and analogical processes.
Emotional responses are critical because people not only think about trust, they also feel it (Fine & Holyﬁeld, 1996).
Emotions can guide behavior when rules fail to apply and when cognitive resources are not available to support a calculated rational choice.

kp.k: Interpersonal trust findings require cautious translation to automation
kp.d: The review identifies differences in intentionality, reciprocal awareness and perceived responsibility. Automation embodies designers' purposes, but users may also attribute human motives to it. In Lewandowsky et al. (2000), participants delegated pump control either to automation or to what they believed was another operator, although the same controller operated in both conditions. Delegation to the supposed human involved concerns about how others perceived the participant, while trust was more strongly related to delegation to automation.
qs: A fundamental challenge in extrapolating from this research to trust in automation is that automation lacks intentionality.
There is no such symmetry in the trust between people and machines, and this leads people to trust and respond to automation differently.
They also found the degree of trust to be more strongly related to the decision to delegate to the automation, as compared with the decision to delegate to the human.

kp.k: Trust does not develop through fixed sequential stages
kp.d: The authors reject a universal progression from performance-based trust to process-based trust and finally faith. Automation users may receive a statement of purpose before observing performance, making purpose the initial basis of trust. Documentation, interfaces and training determine which information is available; similar departures from sequential development occur in temporary groups and virtual teams.
qs: Like trust between people, trust in automation develops according to the information available, rather than following a ﬁxed series of stages.
The speciﬁc evolution depends on the type of information provided by the human-computer interface and the documentation and training.

kp.k: Reliance and trust form a self-reinforcing feedback loop
kp.d: Using automation generates observations that can change trust, while distrust can prevent use and block learning about capabilities. Conversely, high trust may reduce monitoring, allowing faults to go unnoticed. The authors propose that these feedback effects help explain nonlinear reliance, divergent individual trajectories and situations in which trust appears either fragile or robust.
qs: If the system is not trusted, it is unlikely to be used; if it is not used, the operator may have limited information regarding its capabilities, and it is unlikely that trust will grow.
Also, highly trusted automation may be monitored less frequently (Muir & Moray, 1996), and so trust may continue to grow even if occasional faults occur.
A small difference in the predisposition to trust may have a substantial effect when it inﬂuences an initial decision to engage the automation.

kp.k: Automation type determines opportunities to observe and learn
kp.d: The review distinguishes information acquisition, information analysis, decision selection and action implementation. Information-acquisition aids may remain observable without reliance, whereas action-implementation automation often cannot be observed after manual control is adopted, potentially impeding trust recovery. Separately, Meyer (2001) distinguishes compliance with explicit abnormal-condition warnings from reliance on indications of normal operation and reports greater caution with compliance-oriented automation.
qs: Four types of automation have important implications for the dynamics of trust: information acquisition, information analysis, decision selection, and action implementation (Parasuraman, Sheridan, & Wickens, 2000).
In contrast, it is not possible for operators to observe action implementation automation unless they are relying on it, as in automation that controls a pump (Lee & Moray, 1994).
With compliance-oriented automation (e.g., a hazard warning), the automation indicates an abnormal situation, and the operators act in response to this indicator.

kp.k: Trust responds to failures with delays and inertia
kp.d: The review distinguishes acute, transient failures from chronic deficiencies. Trust declines and recovers over time rather than instantaneously. It reports that a time-series equation in Lee and Moray (1994) accounted for between 60% and 86% of variance in overall reliance patterns. The authors propose dynamical analysis to study delayed adjustment, instability and direction-dependent responses; these are methodological recommendations rather than universal predictive results.
qs: The effect of faults on trust is not instantaneous; faults cause trust to decline over time.
This time-series equation accounted for between 60% and 86% of the variance in the overall patterns of operators’ reliance on automation (Lee & Moray, 1994).
This analysis also shows that trust and reliance has inertia, which may be a critical element in understanding reliance on automation (Farrell & Lewandowsky, 2000; Lee & Moray).

kp.k: Failure predictability matters alongside reliability and severity
kp.d: Reported studies show that negative experiences and early reliability can disproportionately shape later trust. Predictable systematic faults may be accommodated, whereas small unpredictable faults can be more damaging to trust. Reported reliability drop-off estimates range from 90% to 70% to 60% across different studies and settings; the authors explicitly reject a universal reliability threshold for distrust or disuse.
qs: A small fault with unpredictable results affected trust more than did a large fault of constant error (Moray et al.; Muir & Moray, 1996).
Trust can develop when a systematic fault occurs for which a control strategy can be developed.
No single level of reliability can be identiﬁed that will lead to distrust and disuse; instead, trust depends on the timing, consequence, and expectations associated with failures of the automation.

kp.k: Self-confidence and workload shape reliance independently of trust
kp.d: Studies reviewed associate high self-confidence and low automation trust with manual control, and low self-confidence with greater automation use. Navigation-system errors reduced trust and reliance more in familiar than unfamiliar cities. The authors also note that configuration effort and time constraints can make non-use appropriate even when automation is capable and trusted; recommendations to allocate final authority to automation concern some time-critical situations, not all work.
qs: When operators’ self-conﬁdence is high and trust in the system is low, they are more inclined to rely on manual control.
The demands of conﬁguring and engaging automation may make reliance inappropriate even when trust is high and the automation is very capable (Kirlik, 1993).
Understanding the role of trust in the decision to rely on automation requires a consideration of the operating context that goes beyond trust alone.

kp.k: Multitasking can impair monitoring of highly reliable automation
kp.d: The review reports poorer failure detection when operators monitor reliable automation alongside other tasks, with similar findings among highly experienced pilots and with infrequent faults. It presents both excessive trust and rational allocation of scarce monitoring resources as possible explanations. In one adaptive-automation flight simulation, returning monitoring to manual control for 10 min improved subsequent failure detection.
qs: In contrast, when the operators’ only task was to monitor the automation, they detected almost all failures (Thackray & Touchstone, 1989).
Another explanation is that operators adopt a eutactic monitoring pattern that can be considered optimal because it balances the costs of monitoring and the probability of failures (Moray, 2003).
The 10 min in manual control substantially improved subsequent detection of automation failures (Parasuraman, Mouloua, & Molloy, 1996).

kp.k: Context-sensitive capabilities require context-sensitive training and trust
kp.d: Automation may perform differently across weather, maintenance conditions and operational situations. The review reports that situation-specific reliability training and knowledge of imperfect predictor information helped users calibrate trust and allocate attention. Fault effects can be specific to individual controllers rather than spreading to independent controllers. The authors recommend showing how past performance varies by situation and evaluating functional and temporal specificity.
qs: The environmental context not only influences trust and reliance, it can also inﬂuence the performance of the automation: The automation may perform well in certain circumstances and not in others.
A fault in the automation did not cause trust to decline in other similar, but functionally independent, automatic controllers (Lee & Moray, 1992; Muir & Moray, 1996).
Training to promote appropriate trust should address how situations interact with the characteristics of the automation to affect its capability.

kp.k: Individual differences do not equate trust with gullibility
kp.d: The authors report that high interpersonal trust was not associated with greater gullibility and that trusting individuals sometimes judged trustworthiness more accurately. In Singh, Molloy and Parasuraman (1993), high-complacency participants detected 53.4% of automation failures versus 18.7% for low-complacency participants under constant reliability. The suggestion that high-trust users might adjust trust more effectively is explicitly identified as a hypothesis requiring investigation.
qs: Interestingly, high-trust individuals are not more gullible than low-trust individuals (Gurtman, 1992), and the propensity to trust is not correlated with measures of intellect (Rotter, 1980); however, high-trust individuals are viewed as more trustworthy by others and display more truthful behavior (Rotter,1971).

For example, Singh, Molloy, and Parasuraman (1993) found that high-complacency individuals actually detected more automation failures in a constant reliability condition (53.4% compared with 18.7% for low-complacency individuals).

kp.k: Organizational culture and indirect experience influence trust
kp.d: The review describes how prior experience, professional roles, reputation, gossip and cultural expectations influence initial trust and interpretation of evidence. It cites greater automation trust and reliance among pilots than unfamiliar students and warns against unqualified cross-cultural generalization. The authors stress that direct human-automation research on these contextual factors remained limited and recommend addressing informal accounts of capability during training.
qs: The organizational context reﬂects the interactions between people that inform them about the trustworthiness of others, which can include reputation and gossip.
The culturally dependent nature of trust suggests that ﬁndings regarding trust in automation may need to be verified when they are extrapolated from one cultural setting to another.
Some evidence shows that these relationships may also hold for trust in automation; however, very little research has investigated any of these factors.

kp.k: Interface polish can increase trust without increasing capability
kp.d: The review reports effects of photographs, layout, realism, speech consistency and other surface characteristics on credibility and reliance. A website survey included more than 1400 people. Target-detection studies associated realistic imagery with greater reliance, while reliability-coded luminance helped users weight sources appropriately. The authors caution that anthropomorphic speech or persuasive presentation can induce false expectations, and that supporting information must fit available decision time.
qs: In many cases, trust and credibility depend on surface features of the interface that have no obvious link to the true capabilities of the system (Briggs, Burford, & Dracup, 1998; Tseng & Fogg, 1999).
Increasing image realism increased trust and led to greater reliance on the cueing information (Yeh & Wickens, 2001).
Although reliance and trust depend on the supporting information provided by the system, the amount of information must be tailored to the available decision time (Entin, Entin, & Serfaty, 1996).

kp.k: Trustable design makes capabilities and limitations understandable
kp.d: The authors distinguish reliable, efficient 'trustworthy' automation from 'trustable' automation that supports appropriately calibrated reliance. Their tentative guidance includes displaying past performance, comprehensible intermediate results, algorithms, intended purpose and application limits, alongside training in reliability and mechanisms. They propose investigating whether simpler but less capable systems can sometimes outperform complex systems at the joint human-automation level by enabling better reliance.
qs: Trustable automation supports adaptive reliance on the automation through highly calibrated, high-resolution, and highspeciﬁcity trust.
Show the process and algorithms of the automation by revealing intermediate results in a way that is comprehensible to the operators.
Trustworthy automation is automation that performs efficiently and reliably.
The trade-off between trustworthy and trustable automation and the degree to which interface design and training can mitigate this trade-off merit investigation.

kp.k: Shared automation introduces unresolved team-level trust problems
kp.d: The authors identify multiperson management of automation as an unexplored research area in 2004. Team members need appropriate trust in the automation, in colleagues who may assume manual control and in whether colleagues' own automation trust is appropriate. They call this last relationship 'meta trust' and propose studying how communication networks and direct experience shape the diffusion of trust.
qs: Research has not yet considered the evolution of trust in multiperson groups that share responsibility for managing automation.
Meta trust refers to the trust a person has that the other person’s trust in the automation is appropriate.
Multiperson, computer-mediated management of automation represents an unexplored area with considerable implications for many emerging systems.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Lee and See argue that increasingly complex automation makes appropriately calibrated trust central to safe and effective human–automation cooperation, rather than simply requiring greater trust.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain review of automation, not a study of legal services or contemporary generative AI. The authors argue that automation can extend human performance and improve safety, but inappropriate reliance can undermine safety and profitability through misuse and disuse. Trust influences reliance without determining it. Their conceptual model describes trust as a dynamic response to information about automation's performance, process and purpose, mediated by analytic, analogical and affective processes. Appropriate trust can enable joint human–automation performance superior to either alone. They recommend interfaces and training that communicate capabilities, limitations and context, and warn that realistic imagery or conversational interfaces can increase trust without corresponding increases in capability. They also raise, as a research proposition rather than an established result, the possibility that simpler, more understandable automation can sometimes be preferable to more capable but less understandable automation. They predict that trust will become more important as automation grows more complex and pervasive.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors synthesize laboratory experiments, simulations, field observations, accident accounts and interdisciplinary trust research; the article supplies a conceptual model and tentative design guidance, not a new automation-performance benchmark.
pts.d: Lee and See draw on research in aviation, maritime navigation, process control, driving, target detection and online interactions. They use the Airbus A320 and Royal Majesty accidents as illustrations of excessive reliance, and Zuboff's observations of rejected paper-mill controllers as an illustration of disuse. They report that Lee and Moray's 1994 time-series equation accounted for 60%–86% of variance in overall patterns of operators' reliance. Experiments on multitasking and automation monitoring support the claim that reliable automation can be associated with missed failures; an adaptive-automation study found that a 10-minute return to manual monitoring improved subsequent failure detection. Interface research supports the claim that surface features can influence trust independently of capability. Findings from interpersonal trust and neuroscience provide additional theoretical support, but the authors explicitly caution against unqualified transfer to automation and identify gaps concerning affect-oriented design, culture and teams. Their forward-looking claims and simpler-versus-more-capable trade-off are proposals or extrapolations rather than demonstrated general outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Published in 2004, the review describes existing automation and makes undated predictions about its increasing pervasiveness; its central claims are conditional on uncertainty, complexity, context and user constraints.
pts.d: The authors specify no calendar deadline for the predicted increase in trust's importance. Trust is especially relevant when users cannot exhaustively understand or evaluate automation and must adapt to unexpected circumstances. Reliance also depends on self-confidence, workload, perceived risk, effort required to engage automation and time constraints. Trust changes with use, feedback, failures and recovery; failure timing, predictability and consequences matter, so there is no universal reliability threshold for disuse. Recommendations depend on communicating context-specific capabilities in cognitively usable forms, not merely making information available. The authors caution that findings from interpersonal trust and particular cultural or laboratory settings require care when generalized. They also argue that final authority for some time-critical decisions should be allocated to automation, rather than assuming human intervention is always feasible.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are operators, designers, trainers, organizations and consumers using or depending on automation—not specifically lawyers or legal-market participants.
pts.d: Pilots, maritime crews, process-plant operators, drivers, air-traffic controllers and users of automated decision aids face changes in delegation, monitoring, workload and exposure to failures. Organizations can lose safety and profitability benefits when automation is overused or rejected. Designers and trainers are asked to support calibrated, function-specific and context-sensitive trust rather than maximize acceptance. Coworkers and teams influence reliance through reputation, informal communication and shared responsibility; the authors identify trust in colleagues' management of automation as an underexplored issue. Their consumer-facing prediction concerns home automation, personal robots and automotive automation. No claims about legal employment, law-firm staffing, legal pricing or access to justice are made.
